name: Grey Pink
lede: Grey pink is a descriptive color name, a pink greyed down until it is dusty, and it has more to say about how we name colors than about any one history.

sections.title: A name built from two mixtures
sections.body:
Grey pink is not a pigment or a place; it is plain grammar, a modifier set before a base word. Batchelor points out that grey and pink are both colors you can describe as mixtures, pink being a pale or whitish red and grey likewise a mixture of other colors, which makes this name a mixture of mixtures [1]. Its first appearances in our sources are charts, not stories: Ridgway's 1912 plate XXVII and the ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955, which calls the swatch a light grayish purplish red, 4.5 units away [2].

The taste for such dusty tones is older than the name. Pastoureau describes an eighteenth-century dyeing manual of 632 pages, of which about 60 cover mordants and blends for purples, oranges, greys, pinks and browns, and he reads it as the sign of a growing taste for pastel shades [3].

sections.title: Near neighbors
sections.body: The closest named color is [[puce]], 3.8 units away, and the library files Light Mauve and Vinaceous as alternatives for the same swatch [2]. On the warm side it also sits close to [[mountbatten-pink]]; St Clair describes the hulls of a passenger-ship line as an indeterminate dull lavender-gray-pink, in the pages that lead into that color's story [4]. Where [[pink]] is clear, this is [[grey]] with a flush of rose in it.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Grey pink is rare in paint: 38 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.16 per cent), 20 by the stricter within-painting lens, rarer than 61 per cent of named colors [5]. Its most frequent role is a hidden color, in 60 per cent of those 20, one that reads as a quiet note beneath louder ones [5].

It peaks in the 1600s, in 6 of 6,394 paintings, 1.2 times the baseline [5]. The earliest match is a work of 1520, a look-alike hue 392 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, 1912 [5]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [5]

questions.q: In paintings where grey pink appears, which role does it most often play?

openers: Grey pink is a name made of two mixtures: pink is already a pale red, and grey a mixture of other colors.
Look for it as a hidden color: in 60 per cent of the paintings where it appears, it plays a quiet supporting role.
